decisions.quote:
Evidence that affective factors (e.g. anxiety, depression, affect) are significantly related to individual differences in emotion recognition is mixed. Palermo et al. (Palermo et al. 2018 J. Exp. Psychol. Hum. Percept. Perform.
44, 503–517) reported that individuals who scored lower in anxiety performed significantly better on two measures of facial-expression recognition (emotion-matching and emotion-labelling tasks), but not a third measure (the multimodal emotion recognition test). By contrast, facial-expression recognition was not significantly correlated with measures of depression, positive or negative affect, empathy, or autistic-like traits. Because the range of affective factors considered in this study and its use of multiple expression-recognition tasks mean that it is a relatively comprehensive investigation of the role of affective factors in facial expression recognition, we carried out a direct replication.
decisions.location: Primary abstract and full Introduction/Methods/Discussion; all shipped rows951/2156 checked
decisions.reason: Full primary article explicitly carries out the Palermo2018 facial-expression/anxiety retest, already correctly represented in row951 (DOI10.1037/xhp0000463). Row2156 instead supplies Berggren/Eimer visual-search paper10.1037/xhp0000541 while quoting the same Palermo finding. Entire primary retest/design/reference chain selects Palermo; substituting Palermo into2156 would duplicate951. Retain951, remove2156; no extra missing reference or second outcome transfer. Independent parent source inspection, not the initial expert replacement proposal.
